title.en: Act II: the murder and its discovery

hook.en: In Act II the murder happens off stage, but we feel every second of it: a vision, a bell, a knocking at the gate, and a dawn that will not break.

objectives.en: Follow the events of the murder night and the morning after
Analyse the dagger vision, the knocking and the guilt of the Macbeths
Explain how the murder disturbs the natural order

narration.en: In Act II the murder happens off stage, but we feel every second of it: a vision, a bell, a knocking at the gate, and a dawn that will not break.

body.en: Late at night Banquo, unable to sleep, tells Macbeth he dreamt of the Witches; Macbeth pretends he thinks little of them. Alone, Macbeth sees a vision of a dagger leading him to Duncan's room, which he cannot grasp: a sign of his disturbed mind. A bell, rung by his wife, is his signal. After the murder he is shaken: he could not say "Amen", he thinks he heard a voice cry that he has murdered sleep, and he has brought the daggers away. Lady Macbeth calmly returns them and smears the sleeping grooms with blood, saying a little water will clear them of the deed.

points.en: The imagined dagger: a mind in turmoil
Macbeth is horrified after the murder
Lady Macbeth returns the daggers and blames the grooms

text.en: Night falls
Banquo cannot rest; he hides his unease;
Macbeth claims to care little for the Witches.
The vision
Alone, Macbeth sees a dagger in the air
leading him on; the bell rings.
Climax
The murder, off stage; Macbeth returns shaken;
his wife takes the daggers back.
Discovery
Knocking; the Porter; Macduff finds the king;
Macbeth kills the grooms in "fury".
Aftermath
The sons flee and fall under suspicion;
nature is disordered; Macbeth will be crowned.

body.en: The two Macbeths react differently: he is overwhelmed by guilt and fear, she is practical and dismissive, a contrast that later reverses. The Porter scene, where a drunk porter pretends to be the gatekeeper of hell, brings comic relief but also reminds us that the castle has become a kind of hell. Macduff discovers the body; Macbeth kills the grooms, claiming loyal fury, which Macduff notes with suspicion. Duncan's sons flee, fearing for their lives, and are blamed. Unnatural events in nature mirror the unnatural crime.

points.en: He is guilty and fearful; she is practical
The Porter: comic relief and a hell-gate image

explanation.en: Shakespeare uses images and sounds to show guilt and disorder rather than showing the murder itself.

problem.en: Contrast the reactions of Macbeth and Lady Macbeth immediately after the murder.

steps.en: Macbeth is terrified and full of remorse: he dwells on what he heard and on his bloody hands.
He is too shaken to return the daggers.
Lady Macbeth calls his fears foolish, takes the daggers back and smears the grooms.
She thinks water will clean away the deed; later events will show how wrong she is.

answer.en: He is overwhelmed by guilt; she is calm and practical, for now.
